item.title: ‘Better Chemistry’: Has the Trump-Zelensky Relationship Thawed?
item.description:
President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine met President Trump at the White House on Tuesday as their relationship appears stronger than ever before — even as both men face challenges at home.

At the meeting, Mr. Zelensky, still confronting domestic fallout over sacking both his defense minister and army chief, was hoping to reboot stalled peace talks in Ukraine’s war against Russia and to push for more U.S. help with weapons, particularly air defense. It was likely, analysts said, that the men would discuss the potential of a cease-fire in long-range airstrikes between Russia and Ukraine.

Mr. Zelensky will also attend the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham, who died suddenly on July 11, hours after returning from Ukraine. The South Carolina Republican was perhaps Ukraine’s biggest ally in Mr. Trump’s circle, whose members have typically echoed Russian talking points.

Some analysts have speculated that Mr. Graham’s death might push Mr. Trump to be more sympathetic toward Ukraine. Some have also taken note of the visit this month to Ukraine by the right-wing activist Laura Loomer, part of the MAGA movement, who has recently expressed support for Ukraine.

Others said Mr. Trump wanted to revive peace talks because he needed a diplomatic win and because reaching a lasting cease-fire in the U.S. war on Iran has proved elusive.

“The relationship with Iran is still very much fragile,” said Harry Nedelcu, a senior director at Rasmussen Global, a European political advisory firm. So, he added, “Ukraine comes to the forefront.”

“But most importantly for both men,” he continued, “this is a moment where they could validate each other’s diplomatic efforts and leverage each other. Trump could leverage Zelensky, and Zelensky could help him validate his own administration at a time when domestically, Trump is not doing very well.”

The two leaders have long had a tricky relationship. Their meeting at the White House at the beginning of Mr. Trump’s second term was a disaster, punctuated by Mr. Zelensky’s being asked to leave. The Trump administration has consistently leaned toward Russia in peace negotiations, saying Mr. Zelensky did not have the cards to win. Under Mr. Trump, the United States cut off almost all military aid to Ukraine.

Mr. Zelensky has worked hard to mollify Mr. Trump in subsequent meetings. And Ukraine has fared better against Russia this year than expected, largely because of its drone advances. Ukraine is projecting the kind of strength that Mr. Trump typically favors.

The United States has also turned to Ukraine for help with drones and with drone interceptors, particularly in the war on Iran.

Got a confidential news tip? The New York Times would like to hear from readers who want to share messages and materials with our journalists.

“There is a better chemistry now I see between them,” said Volodymyr Dubovyk, director of the Center for International Studies at Odesa National University in Ukraine.

“Maybe Zelensky understands Trump a little better,” he added. “Maybe Trump understands Zelensky a little bit better.”

Ukraine has even peripherally entered the fray in the Iran war, hitting an Iranian ship in the Caspian Sea with a long-range drone on Saturday. Iran, which has long provided drone technology to Russia that is used against Ukraine, said the ship was a commercial vessel, vowed retaliation and accused Ukraine of deliberately widening the war. Mr. Zelensky said Kyiv had struck a cargo vessel moving military supplies between Iran and Russia.

While Ukraine’s long-range drones have also caused damage in parts of Russia, Ukraine is at a significant disadvantage in the air war. So far in July, Russia has fired 117 ballistic missiles at Ukrainian cities, according to a New York Times data set based on numbers from the Ukrainian Air Force, almost a monthly record.

Mr. Zelensky has repeatedly asked for more U.S.-made Patriot interceptor missiles — the only air defense system Ukraine possesses that is capable of shooting down Russia’s ballistic missiles. This month, in another positive sign for Ukraine, Mr. Trump agreed to allow Ukraine to produce the interceptors, although ramping up production will take years.

Ms. Loomer, who often talks to Mr. Trump, is emblematic of the shift in thinking on the war from part of Mr. Trump’s base.

Like others in the MAGA movement, she used to regularly espouse Russian talking points and oppose U.S. aid for Ukraine. But this year, Ms. Loomer said in an interview with The New York Times, she started questioning her beliefs, describing a “woke right” of influential media figures including Tucker Carlson who had swallowed Russian propaganda on Ukraine and were undermining American national security.

Last week, she made a surprise visit to Ukraine, traveling about 35 hours from her home in Florida to the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv. On Thursday, Ms. Loomer interviewed Mr. Zelensky in a garden near the presidential residence, acknowledging that she felt a moral obligation to correct the record.

Ms. Loomer, who said she had repeatedly gone to bomb shelters during air raid sirens, said on Saturday that she had called Mr. Trump twice from Ukraine.

“He said, ‘Oh, tell Zelensky I said hello,’” Ms. Loomer recounted as her team drove from the eastern city of Kharkiv to Kyiv, stopping at military checkpoints and to film a video at a bombed-out gas station.

“And then, you know, I knew that Zelensky would be at the White House next week, and Zelensky had nothing but nice things to say,” Ms. Loomer added, noting that she intended to spend another week in Ukraine visiting factories and military sites.

After she posted a preview of her interview with Mr. Zelensky online, Mr. Trump shared it on his social media site. “Very good!!!” he said.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

While Ms. Loomer says Mr. Trump likes both Mr. Zelensky and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, she also says Mr. Trump realizes Mr. Putin is the problem.

“I think the tide is really changing,” she said. She added later in the interview, “I really honestly do believe that Ukraine, over time, could end up being one of our greatest allies.”

Natalia Yermak contributed reporting.

item.title: ‘A Wake-Up Call’: Massive Wildfires Pierce Madrid’s Bubble
item.description:
As the worst wildfires in Spanish history tore through the country, Elena Sánchez paused from selling beers in a kiosk on the edge of an artificial lake in Madrid and pointed west toward the sunset. It was the wrong color.

“It’s not supposed to be like that,” Ms. Sánchez, 54, said on Sunday evening, looking at a hazy gray blush — the fire’s smoky residue — in the not-so-distant distance.

As fires raged 30 miles from Madrid in recent days, an acrid burning smell imbued all of this park on Madrid’s western edge, Ms. Sánchez said. Though the situation improved over the weekend, people initially stopped exercising for the itching in their throats, she said, and older residents wore surgical masks outdoors. She could still feel the smoke on her tongue, she said.

“It’s scary,” Ms. Sánchez said. “I’m afraid it might reach here.”

In recent years, wealthy expats, immigrant workers and global attention have made Madrid a booming European capital. But as the flames on Monday reached new areas around the capital and extended to more regions around the country, a suffocating reality check has also reached the city.

In a country led by a government that has defined itself by the seriousness with which it takes climate change, the flames have come unsettlingly close to the capital. The fires around Madrid have brought to tears the region’s president, Isabel Díaz Ayuso. Experts say they are a harbinger for the damage to come on the world’s fastest warming continent.

“These are difficult hours,” Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said Monday afternoon during a news conference in Castellón, on Spain’s eastern coast, where a new fire raged and forced thousands of new evacuations.

In the face of what his government has called the largest fires in the country’s history, and after a summer of record-breaking heat waves, he called for a national pact with all Spain’s political parties to work together to prevent blazes that he attributed to climate change. “This climate emergency is exceeding every threshold and scale that scientists have long warned all of Spain and Europe about,” he said.

On Monday, regional authorities ordered the evacuation of Valdemaqueda, a town of about 870 people roughly 25 miles away from the Spanish capital, another sign that the wildfires west of Madrid were not fully under control. Fernando Grande-Marlaska, Spain’s interior minister, said that firefighters had a “crucial” two-day window to control the fires around Madrid before extreme temperatures topping 100 Fahrenheit were expected to wallop the country.

All that has shaken Madrid’s residents, who can’t remember when such a large fire came so close to the city.

“This is a wake-up call,” said Leopoldo Salvador, 84, who walked under a statue of Don Quixote in the Plaza España, a central square in Madrid. He said he closed the windows of his house over the temperate weekend to keep the smoke out.

Near the city’s royal palace, Cristina Herrero, 46, a biology professor at the Complutense University of Madrid, listened on her phone to news about the fires. She and her friends walked by the palace gardens with sheep dogs that they had evacuated from their farms outside the city.

“I’m sorry,” Ms. Herrero called out to another dogwalker as her pack barked and growled at the unleashed dogs around them. “These are evacuated dogs!”

As the other dogwalker gave her a dirty look, she talked about the sheep and horses and beehives she had left behind in the farms outside the city. Ms. Herrero said that while the city still felt insulated and safe, those living just to the capital’s west were “very worried.”

Her friend Henar Hidalgo Riol, 60, who was also walking an evacuated dog, agreed.

“There are fires everywhere,” Ms. Hidalgo Riol said, adding that dry brush carpeted the mountains surrounding Madrid. “People know they’re sitting on a powder keg.”

Experts said the fires resulted partly from the loss of rural culture that had required forest management. Less grazing and less logging meant woods and landscapes throughout Spain, and in greater Madrid, were left untouched, a potentially explosive ingredient when combined with dry conditions that are made more likely by the burning of fossil fuels.

“Fires now find fuel everywhere,” said Víctor Resco, professor of forest engineering in the University of Lleida.

Outside the royal palace on Monday, Charo Fernández, 65, a lawyer, strolled toward a horizon that looked like a mountain range but was the faint silhouette of smoke from the fires to the west. She said her clothes reeked of smoke over the weekend, and that smoke had billowed from the west and toward the city as if “out of a chimney.”

Those signs of fire were like nothing Ms. Sánchez, who works at the kiosk by the lake, said she had ever seen. She said that Madrid’s weeks of record-breaking heat had already exhausted her, and that climate change seemed unstoppable. No matter what resources and legislation the country threw at the fires.

“It just keeps spreading,” she said, looking at the sullied sunset. “Just don’t let it reach here.”

Carlos Barragán contributed reporting.

item.title: Why Iran Is in No Rush to Return to Talks With United States
item.description:
For the past several days, Iran’s skies have been free of the sound of explosions and airstrikes after nearly two weeks of renewed fighting with the United States. But Iranian officials have said they have not agreed to a cease-fire, and that they are in no hurry to talk directly to the Americans.

Instead, Iranian officials have emphasized that they are in a position of strength, with military officials boasting about their success on the battlefield and diplomats dismissing U.S. claims that they are eager to return to negotiations.

The rhetoric coming from Tehran is an indication that Iran’s leaders appear comfortable with the limbo state of its war with the United States, believing that they can handle a return to conflict and that they have leverage over President Trump. The outcome that Iran seems to be prioritizing is recognition of its control over the Strait of Hormuz, a concession that the United States has been unwilling to make.

Despite the bluster, the uncertainty over whether war or peace will reign at any moment is a challenge for Iran, analysts say. Fighting could break out again at any time, a final settlement appears distant and Iran’s economy is likely to further deteriorate because of the instability, wartime destruction and a U.S. naval blockade.

Ramazan Sharif, a former spokesman for the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, the ideological military force that has solidified its control over Iran during the war, said on Sunday that Iran’s “enemy” had “faced strategic defeat at every step,” Iranian state media reported.

Iranian diplomats reacted with more restraint to the pause in the fighting, but hardly expressed that they were in a mood for compromise.

“At present, what exists cannot be described as a cease-fire,” the Iranian foreign ministry spokesman, Esmail Baghaei, said at a news conference on Monday, after the fighting had stopped for several days.

Mr. Trump claimed on Monday that Iran had asked for a pause to meet for talks, and that the two sides were engaged in discussions.

Mr. Baghaei denied that. “We currently have no negotiations with the United States,” he said, though he acknowledged that Pakistan and Qatar were mediating between the two sides in comments to Austria’s public broadcaster, that were widely quoted by Iranian state media on Sunday.

Mr. Baghaei has called America’s war against Iran a “quagmire they themselves created.”

Iran’s negotiations, he said, were with Oman, over management of the Strait of Hormuz, the critical waterway for oil and gas shipments that Iran effectively shut down after being attacked by the United States and Israel in February.

“They believe that time is on their side, that they can absorb pain and pressure more successfully than Donald Trump can, and that ultimately he will agree to a deal that fits their demands — without any concessions from their side,” said Gregory Brew, a senior analyst on Iran at the Eurasia Group, a political risk advisory firm.

The recent resumption of fighting caused oil prices to surge, raising prices at the gas pump for American consumers. Oil prices have fallen sharply in recent days, after the United States and Iran paused their attacks.

But Iran is at risk of overreaching, Mr. Brew said. For Mr. Trump, escalating the war is more attractive than accepting a deal that gives Iran control over the strait, he added, and other countries are unlikely to accept tolls on ships. There is scope for both sides to de-escalate if Iran can accept a compromise arrangement for the future of the waterway.

“Otherwise, Trump is going to go back to airstrikes — clearly his preferred form of diplomacy — to try and force them to back down, doing more damage to Iran’s battered economy and remaining military capabilities,” Mr. Brew said.
